title.narrative: NIHR RIGHT 7: Cardiovascular disease risk reduction in sub–Saharan Africa (CARisSA)

description.narrative:
A UK and low- and middle-income country (LMIC) research partnership that aims to develop and evaluate a community-centred intervention for cardiovascular disease (CVD) risk reduction is proposed. This partnership, involving experts from the UK, Kenya, and The Gambia, focuses on addressing high CVD risks in sub-Saharan Africa (SSA), especially in regions where CVD management is challenging due to limited resources and complex health system barriers.
The project aims to design and test a contextualised, multi-component intervention that combines task-sharing with community health workers, digital health tools, combination therapy, and peer support groups to manage overall CVD risk in high-burden SSA areas.
The project is led by the London School of Hygiene & Tropical Medicine (LSHTM), Wellcome Trust Kenya Research Programme (KWTRP), and the Medical Research Council Unit The Gambia (MRCG). Joint Principal Investigators include Professor Pablo Perel and Associate Professor Anthony Etyang, alongside a collaborative team of local healthcare providers, community health workers, and international CVD experts. The research will take place in Kilifi County, Kenya, and Kiang West, The Gambia. These regions are selected due to their high CVD burden and existing research infrastructure that facilitates effective data collection and intervention implementation.
The project is scheduled to run from 2025 to 2029, with initial co-design phases in 2025, followed by feasibility testing, a full-scale trial, and process evaluation until the final impact assessment phase. CVD rates are high in SSA, with younger populations at risk due to untreated hypertension and other risk factors. This project aims to address significant gaps in CVD risk management by implementing cost-effective, evidence-based solutions that are sustainable within the local health systems. The long-term goal is to improve CVD outcomes and facilitate scalability and adoption across similar high-burden regions in SSA.
